newsitem.title: UK: Syria seeks price rise but lifters fret over Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Syria seeks price rise but lifters fret over Iraq.

text.p: Syria is seeking higher prices for its crude oil in July encouraged by buoyant sour markets in the Mediterranean, but customers worried that Iraqi exports could resume in the middle of the month are resisting for fear spot prices would tumble.
State-owned Sytrol has telexed term contract holders with an opening offer of Dated Brent -55 cents a barrel for its key Syrian Light crude, an increase of 22 cents over June.
But regular lifters of Syrian crude are wary of signing up for a higher price for the whole of July, given the chance of renewed Iraqi exports which could prompt a sharp slide.
Most are seeking a rollover of June's Dated Brent -77 cents a barrel, although a modest increase would be acceptable to some.

"It's a very tricky situation at the moment. There will be no spot (Iraqi) barrels available until at least the middle of July but then there could be a flood of crude in a very short period," said one.

The oil-for-food deal was renewed two weeks ago but Baghdad has said oil sales for the second six month period beginning June 8 cannot begin until the proceeds from the first tranche of exports held in an escrow account have been spent.
Sytrol argues that rival sours have rallied dramatically this month and it wants July prices to reflect at least part of the gains.

Regional benchmark Russian Urals has seen its discount to Dated Brent slashed by 40 cents since the beginning of June amid growing uncertainty about when exports of Iraqi Kirkuk Blend will resume from the Turkish port of Ceyhan.
Southern European refineries have been left scrabbling around for alternatives, forcing sour markets higher.
But the green light from Baghdad would mean an almost immediate resumption of deliveries to Turkish refineries and loadings at Ceyhan as soon as freight could be arranged.
"They've got ten million barrels in storage at Ceyhan and pipeline deliveries can begin as soon as the taps are turned on again," said a trader.
Syrian customers also point out that Urals recent strength has squeezed refinery margins with Med cracking yields falling to $1.85 a barrel on Thursday from over $3 on average last week.

Mediterranean sweet crudes are failing to keep pace, however. More lifters of Algeria's Saharan Blend were expected to fall into line with an agreement on Thursday at just below Dated Brent +40 cents for July, traders said.
Saharan Blend was priced at Dated Brent +60/62 cents in June.
Spot markets were thin with prompt supply of Urals scarce ahead of the release of the official July loading programme, expected next week.
